newsitem.title: CAMBODIA: FEATURE-Studies find Cambodian AIDS problem skyrocketing.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-Studies find Cambodian AIDS problem skyrocketing.

text.p: Three new studies on AIDS have found that while most Cambodians are aware of the epidemic, few fully understand its consequences or take action to make themselves less vulnerable to the deadly disease.

Survey results released in the past week by the U.S. Agency for International Development (AID) and the Cambodian Red Cross found that while many men visit prostitutes, only about 15 percent use condoms regularly and even an smaller proportion -- as low as three percent -- use condoms with their wives.

A third study, to be officially released on Friday by Save the Children UK, found that most 11- to 20-year-olds have heard about Acquired Immune Deficiency Syndrome (AIDS), caused by the human immunodeficiency virus (HIV), but many still think it can be transmitted by casual social contact.

Health workers say prostitutes commonly douche with toothpaste in the mistaken belief it will kill sexually transmitted diseases and surveys find three in four people would not care for a relative with AIDS out of fear of infection.
LACK OF SAFE SEX BREEDS EPIDEMIC

"There are very high levels of basic awareness about HIV/AIDS but a lot of confusion about how it is transmitted and fear of transmission through social contact, such as plates, spoons," said Joan Anderson, director of Save the Children UK in Cambodia, in an interview.
Her organisation surveyed 1,006 people aged 11-20 years.

Dr. Ouk Vong Vathiny of the Reproductive Health Association of Cambodia, told Reuters in an interview that her organisation helped carry out the U.S. AID survey of 1,083 people, including prostitutes, women with sexually transmitted diseases, military and police, and found similar results.
In her survey, 48 percent of sex workers surveyed in Phnom Penh were HIV positive, while in the second largest city of Battambang, 40 percent of prostitutes carried the virus that causes AIDS.
In some areas, as many as 15 percent of military personnel were found to be HIV positive.
About 80 percent of police and military had visited a prostitute in the past year, paying about $4 for the visit.
Despite the high rates of HIV -- among the highest in Asia -- only 16 percent of sex workers said their customers regularly used condoms, the U.S. AID survey said.
Men claimed to use condoms with prostitutes about 37 percent of the time, but married men said they used condoms with their wives only about 15 percent of the time, the survey found.

The Cambodian Red Cross study, which surveyed 1,366 people from Phnom Penh and four provinces, found about 40 percent of married men had two or more sex partners. But only three percent of rural men and 5.6 percent of men in Phnom Penh used condoms with their wives, it said.
CAMBODIA: GROUND ZERO FOR AIDS

"If things continue, we (will) have a new 'killing fields' of HIV," says Ouk Vong Vathiny, who like other health workers fears Cambodia could be ground zero for AIDS in Asia, where infection rates are already the highest in the world.
The analogy to the Khmer Rouge's "killing fields" regime, which left more than one million Cambodians dead in the late 1970s, is bleak but not inappropriate, they say.
The United Nations has said more than 100,000 of Cambodia's 10.5 million people are infected with HIV and 30,000 are expected to die by 2000, with deaths escalating thereafter.

About 800,000 Thais are infected with HIV, and that number is expected to rise to more than 1 million by 2000, the Thai Health Ministry said. Up to a million people in Indonesia and 300,000 in Vietnam are expected to be infected with HIV by 2000.

According to Ouk Vong Vathiny, Cambodia is worse off than neighbouring nations fighting the AIDS epidemic because of a lack of financial resources and the thriving sex industry, which continues to grow unchecked.

"In Thailand, they are richer, and social problems are not as severe. In Vietnam...the authorities act very strongly to close down sex workers completely," she said. "But for us, the impact continues to grow more severe."
The outlook for care of AIDS patients is equally grim, health workers say.
The Cambodian Red Cross study found that three out of four respondents would refuse to care for family members with AIDS out of fear of infection.
Worse, few people get qualified treatment for sexually transmitted diseases, the U.S. AID study found, leading to the misuse of antibiotics and virulent strains resistant to some medicines.
"We need a whole reassessment of our educational messages," Dr. Zari John Gill, AIDS coordinator for World Vision in Cambodia, said in an interview with Reuters.
"We have to build personal responsibility."
